2.text: a small boy of his camp neighbor Aiˊo. The boy remained with him three

3.text: years. Then Aiˊo died. His wife resolved to leave the western tundra and

4.text: cross the Kolyma River. She had some kinsmen on the eastern shore with

5.text: whom she wanted to live. Leaving the camp of her master, she took her

6.text: child back and carried him along with her. Aiñaˊɪrg̣ɪn, at the time of adopting

7.text: the boy, had given to Aiˊo a “joyful present” of two well-broken driving-

8.text: reindeer. Now the woman gave them back. Her chief reason for taking her

9.text: child back was that Aiñaˊɪrg̣ɪn had meanwhile lost and squandered away a

10.text: large part of his herd, and still continued to go downward, so that the prospects

11.text: of life for the adopted child were by no means bright.

12.text: When a child has been taken from a brother or a cousin for adoption, the

13.text: new tie soon becomes very strong, and almost equals the natural tie between

14.text: parents and children. Thus, of the people I met, one Qoraˊwg̣ê adopted the

15.text: little son of his younger brother Äqäˊwg̣i, and had him as his own child;

16.text: another man, Eiñewg̣i by name, adopted Aqačaˊut, the son of his second-

17.text: cousin; etc. Old people who have lost their children, however, do not like

18.text: to adopt new children, but prefer to remain alone in their sorrow.

19.text: On the other hand, the ties between the adopting parent and an adopted

20.text: child of quite foreign origin may sometimes become very strong indeed. The

21.text: remarkable tale about Taˊlo, the adopted child of a Taˊn˙ñɪn (Taˊlo, Taˊn˙ñɪn

22.text: rɪmaiñaˊwg̣o), describes how the Taˊn˙ñɪt were pursuing fugitive Chukchee.

23.text: From one sledge a boy had fallen, — a very small boy, who still wore a

24.text: diaper. He fell into the snow, and lay there weeping. The last of the pursuers

25.text: were two brothers. One had children at home; the other had no boys, only

26.text: one single daughter. When they reached that place, the wail of the child

27.text: was heard by them. “Wait a little,” said the childless one, “let me go and

28.text: see what voice is wailing in the snow.” He found the boy. “Oh, oh, a boy!

29.text: I had better return home: go on by yourself.” He took the boy to his camp.

30.text: There he brought him up as his own son. Taˊlo grew up very quickly.

31.text: Every day he became larger and stronger. Then the adopting father said

32.text: to him, “Oh, my son! I am old and weak. Now try your hand with the

33.text: herd. Here is a girl, a stranger girl, whom I have brought up for you.

34.text: Take her to wife, and both of you be the masters of the camp.” Taˊlo left

35.text: the sleeping-room and went to the herd. From that time on he did not come

36.text: home. All the time, from morning till evening, he ran about without inter-

37.text: ruption, exercising with his lance, shooting with his bow, carrying weights.

38.text: He became as light and nimble as a two-year-old reindeer-buck, the offspring

39.text: of a wild male. At last he was able to jump up into the air like a bird.

40.text: Thus lived Taˊlo. One time his supposed cousins said among themselves,

41.text: “Let us go and have a look at the adopted offspring of the hostile tribe.”

42.text: They came to Taˊlo’s herd, and looked stealthily from behind the bushes.
